content: This includes assessing user accuracy and generating quality control reports based on user interactions and implementation. Feedback from users on the content, identification of incorrect schedules or content updates, timestamps on form submissions, and the number of forms submitted per worker are critical metrics. Additionally, data patterns across workers and geographic areas should be analyzed to identify inconsistencies. This process begins by defining what operating as intended means. For example, if the system includes an SMS application, a guided testing document or QA test cases should be created. Findings from these test cases should inform an iterative process of feedback to developers, further development, and re-testing until a final, field-ready system is achieved. Key aspects to monitor during testing include skip patterns, validation checks, form schedules, form content, user interface (UI) design, data export functionality, data accuracy, and dashboard calculations. Flow diagrams and mock-ups of application interfaces can assist in testing these components. The primary questions to address are whether the system meets the requirements outlined in the system requirements specification (SRS) and whether it fulfills the needs of the health intervention. For example, when a health worker administers a vaccine, the system should accurately record the vaccine as given, display the date, and schedule the next dose appropriately. Monitoring successful functionality requires assigning human resources to this task, which may vary depending on the intervention's maturity stage. In early stages, project managers may handle most of the monitoring, while in later stages, this responsibility can be delegated to trained staff or field supervisors. System functionality monitoring should continue even after launch, especially during the initial weeks and months of implementation, as real-world usage may reveal issues not identified during preliminary testing. Pre-launch findings should be regularly compiled and shared with developers to promptly address any problems. If functionality issues disrupt live intervention services, these disruptions must be documented and considered during the evaluation phase. For instance, if a technical problem prevents SMS vaccination reminders for 15 days, the evaluation must account for the families who missed these reminders. Monitoring requirements differ by maturity stage. Early-stage systems require substantial resources for pre-launch and continued functionality monitoring, as consistent system functionality has not yet been demonstrated. As systems mature, monitoring efforts can focus more on fidelity and quality components. Unstable systems can hinder intervention delivery, such as failing to send vaccination reminder messages or causing users to lose confidence in the system. Stability monitoring can largely be automated after initial testing and during launch. Key metrics to monitor include server outages, SMS failure rates, unexpected application crashes, and system responsiveness under normal and peak data loads. Server logs can help identify events leading to outages, and automated alerts should notify support teams of issues. Monitoring findings should be used to address problems promptly and optimize system performance to prevent future crashes. This involves assessing whether users are completing data collection forms as expected, operating the system correctly, and adhering to health protocols. Systems should be set up for continuous, automated monitoring of server uptime and user activity. For example, monitoring can identify health workers who are not submitting data as frequently as required or who are not following proper procedures. Quality monitoring focuses on two aspects: user capabilities and intervention content. Training large numbers of workers on digital health systems can be challenging due to varying levels of technical literacy and resistance to changing established workflows. Monitoring user readiness involves evaluating their ability to operate the system, enter data accurately, and troubleshoot basic issues. Intervention content, such as SMS messages, decision-support algorithms, and data collection forms, must be of the highest quality, informed by existing literature and tailored to the local context. Before launch, it is crucial to confirm that the intervention content aligns with international standards and is appropriate for the target community. Monitoring findings should guide retraining efforts, address gaps in user understanding, and maintain high-quality content delivery. As interventions progress through maturity stages, monitoring systems must become more automated and sophisticated to handle larger numbers of users and increased data volumes. For example, graphical software or geographic information systems (GIS) dashboards may be needed to visualize performance data for hundreds of workers.
